intro.text: Simple English  •  Real examples  •  Fast revision
A compact guide to the seven Week 1 sections: from software components and requirements to Waterfall, Spiral and Agile. The main explanations follow the topic sequence.

intro.caption: Week 1 at a glance: the major ideas and their connections.

intro.text: First look at the picture. Then read the short explanation. Try the THINK question before reading further. Revise with the comparison and questions at the end.

blocks.text: Software engineering started off as an art: there were good programmers who wrote good code and bad programmers who did not. Over time, the expertise of good programmers was documented, which led to processes, models and strategies for effective software development — and the field of software engineering was born.
Three areas the course covers

rows: E.g. the waterfall model and the agile model, and common practices used in industry
Used by software teams to capture requirements, plan, develop and test
How to organise code and best practices for clean, effective code

blocks.caption: The five main activities in the introductory software development process.

blocks.text: The course follows a learner-centric MOOC model: short videos with reflection spots (pause and write down your thoughts), learning-by-doing activities after videos, discussion forums with focused questions, and extra resources to explore your own interests. Learners are expected to put in at least 6 hours per week. The course project takes you through the entire software development lifecycle, with intermediate milestones each week.
REMEMBER  Software engineering = the expertise of good programmers, organised into processes, models and strategies.

sections.title: Large software is built from components

blocks.text: An online shopping website is not developed as one giant program all at once. Teams often add features gradually. At the beginning, they may not even know every feature that will be needed later.
Component (module)  One manageable part of a big system, such as login, stock management or payment.

blocks.caption: An e-commerce system is divided into parts that work together.

blocks.text: Components break complexity into manageable parts. Different teams build different components and integrate them later. You do not need to know how every component works — only what response it gives when asked. Components hide their implementation and provide an interface.
THINK  Does the Cart team need to understand every line of code in the Payment team? Why not?
Two examples from the chapter

Inventory management is measuring the amount, location, pricing and mix of products available on Amazon. Inventory gets updated based on current purchasing and seasonal trends, fluctuating customer demand, and logistics and analytics. The homepage is also customised based on each user's shopping and viewing history — so my Amazon homepage can be very different from yours.

blocks.caption: Warehouse stock, customer demand and related product recommendations.

blocks.text: A payment gateway is a service that authorizes electronic payments such as online banking, debit cards and cash cards. It acts as a middleman between the bank and the merchant's website or application. When a user wants to pay, the Amazon website sends the encrypted card information to the payment gateway; the gateway confirms the validity of these details with the bank, and the required amount is transferred from the user's account to the Amazon account.

blocks.caption: Amazon sends encrypted card details to the payment gateway, which confirms them with the bank and returns the response.
blocks.alt: Amazon sends encrypted card details to the payment gateway, which confirms them with the bank and returns the response.

blocks.text: REMEMBER  Nobody builds a large system all at once. It is broken into components, called modules, built by different teams and integrated later. Software can be divided into separately addressable components called modules that are integrated to satisfy requirements.

sections.title: Requirement specification: decide WHAT to build

blocks.text: Many people think the first step is learning a programming language. You do need one to write code, but before thinking about the solution you must think about what problem you want to solve.
Requirements: Goals the implemented system should have; they should cater to the needs of clients.

blocks.caption: First understand users and their needs; then plan the feature.

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  Amazon Pay is a mobile wallet — a way to carry cash in digital format. You can link credit/debit cards and bank accounts, or transfer money into it, and pay with your smartphone. It offers recharges, bill payments, travel and insurance, rewards and gift vouchers, and features such as adding money and auto reload.
1. Understand the problem.
2. Study existing components of the system (e.g. inventory management, payment gateway) to see how the new component will interact with them.
3. Look at similar systems (Paytm, PhonePe) to understand features.
4. Write an explicit set of goals = requirements.
A client is not always an outside customer

rows: Mobile banking software serves bank customers – checking account balance, transferring money
An employee resources portal with information about employees and teams; an internal products team builds it, talking to departments like HR to understand requirements
A payment gateway like Razorpay interfaces with an e-commerce website: the site sends customer details, the gateway communicates with the customer's bank and sends the response back to the site

blocks.caption: A client may be an external customer, an internal department or even another software system.

blocks.text: Think about WHO will use the software, for WHAT purpose and in WHAT way — keep this persona of the intended user alive in your mind.

REMEMBER  Requirement specification is the first step in the software development process. Clients are the end users of the software. Requirements must capture clients' needs and be met at every stage — only then will the software meet end users' requirements.

sections.title: Software design: create the big picture

blocks.text: Suppose several developers start coding Amazon Pay without agreeing on the structure. Each person may choose different inputs, data formats or responsibilities. Their parts can fail when connected.

blocks.caption: Without a design, independently built code may not fit together.

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  Developer A changes a function from pay(amount) to pay(amount, currency). Developer B still calls pay(amount). Developer B's module may now fail. Agreeing on interfaces and coordinating changes prevents this confusion.
Such a scenario can be a disaster: it needlessly makes the software complicated and the product will not be delivered on time.
Difficulties while adding new features
If we want to add new features later, it helps to have a big-picture view of the system so we can decide how the new feature can be correctly integrated into the existing system.

blocks.caption: A new feature can be fitted in correctly only when you can see the big picture.

blocks.text: Design is the big-picture view of the software system. It provides a structure to the software system, so we know how to organise the code before we start implementing it.

blocks.caption: A house blueprint is like the design plan for software.

blocks.text: REMEMBER  Requirements say WHAT is needed; design provides the structure for HOW it will be built.

sections.title: Development: write code that fits together

blocks.text: Developers write code based on the requirements and the design. Development is usually distributed — multiple developers work in different locations and even time zones. Tools like GitHub are used to collaborate. Everyone needs a consistent understanding of the code, which is why developers write documentation and precise interface definitions.

blocks.caption: Developers collaborate through code, documentation and shared tools.

blocks.text: Why are documentation and interfaces important?
Documentation explains what a part of the code does.

An interface describes the actions your functions can do without describing the implementation in detail — what requests are accepted and in what format the response (output) is given. The code behind the interface can change as long as the interface remains the same. Simply: it is the language two components use to talk — what form a query should take and what form the answer will take.

blocks.caption: Shopping Cart sends a request; Payment Service returns a result through an interface.

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  The payment service can change its internal implementation, but if the agreed interface stays the same, the cart can still use it. A changed interface may require other modules to change too.
REMEMBER  Team coding succeeds when developers share a clear design and precise interfaces.

sections.title: Testing: check the system before release

blocks.text: Testing ensures the software behaves according to the requirements; many bugs might still exist in the system. Bugs can cost a lot of money: a study showed that in 2002 software bugs cost the US economy around $59.5 billion, and in 2016 this number jumped to $1.1 trillion. Failure to address bugs can even cause severe catastrophes.

blocks.caption: Three testing levels discussed in the chapter.

rows: A single part (usually one class or one function) in total isolation
After testing individual parts, test how parts work together as a whole
Check whether users' requirements are actually met by testing the application with end users

blocks.text: Alpha testing vs Beta testing
Alpha and beta are the two types of acceptance testing.

blocks.caption: Alpha: internal employees in a controlled setting. Beta: actual users in real use.

blocks.text: Alpha: conducted by internal employees in a lab/staging environment; goal: catch as many issues as possible before the product is released to the public.
Beta: conducted by actual users in a real-live setting.
REMEMBER  Unit = one part; Integration = parts together; Acceptance = needs of real users.
After adequate testing the feature is rolled out, but work is not finished. Users may find rare failures, unexpected behavior or problems on certain browsers and devices.

blocks.caption: Maintenance means monitoring usage, changing code and adding features.

blocks.text: 1. Monitor what users are doing and how they use the software: are they using it as intended, and are there any difficulties or errors?
2. Change the code for upgrades/updates (patch releases).
3. Add features.

EXAMPLE  Even after releasing Amazon Pay, some conditions might have been missed, resulting in failures, or there may be a simple UI issue in a very specific browser. The team identifies such issues in the maintenance phase and fixes them.

blocks.caption: Requirements → Design → Development → Testing → Maintenance: the software development process.

blocks.text: REMEMBER  Maintenance includes monitoring, updates and new features - not only bug fixing.

sections.title: Build and Fix: an early coding approach

blocks.text: Many learners have developed software without strictly following requirements → design → code → test. This exploratory programming style is called Build and Fix: programmers start writing the program immediately after forming an informal understanding of the requirements, and once the program is complete they fix anything that does not match the users' expectations. This is how programming was done in the 1950s and 60s. Good programmers knew principles that helped them write good programs — such as thinking about the big-picture view of the system (the design) before writing the program. Over time these good principles and practices, along with research innovations, were systematically organised into software engineering, which emphasises software development as a well-defined and ordered set of activities.

blocks.caption: Build and Fix: begin coding, find problems, patch the code and repeat.

blocks.text: Software lifecycle

The software lifecycle is the different stages, phases and activities over which a software evolves from the initial customer request to a fully developed software. These activities are commonly called the software life cycle model, the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), or the software development process model.

blocks.caption: The software lifecycle and its three common names.

blocks.text: REMEMBER  Build and Fix → good principles + research innovations → software engineering (SDLC).

sections.title: Waterfall: the Plan and Document approach

blocks.text: It is called the waterfall model because each phase occurs one after the other. It is called the Plan and Document perspective because before writing code we come up with a plan for the project, including extensive, detailed documentation of all the phases, and progress is measured against this plan.

blocks.caption: Waterfall: Requirements → Design → Development → Testing → Maintenance.

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  2 months for requirements + 3 for design + 4 for development + 3 for testing = 12 months. At release the client says "I don't like it!!". There may have been a misunderstanding about the requirements, the client may have changed their mind about some requirements, or they may not like the user interface — so the team must go back, refine the requirements and start the process again.

blocks.caption: Twelve months of work, then the client says “I don't like it!!” — back to requirements.

blocks.text: Four drawbacks of the waterfall model
1. Increase in cost and time if changes are required later on.
2. Clients may not know what they need — they might need to see something first.
3. Developers/designers may not know which design is most feasible or usable by clients.
4. Quite long — usually 6–18 months for one cycle.
REMEMBER  Waterfall = plan and document the phases, with a risk of discovering problems late.

sections.title: Prototype Model: show a simple sample early

blocks.text: Build a working prototype of the system before developing the actual software. The prototype has limited functional capabilities, and its performance might not be optimal compared to the actual software. Seeing it makes it easier for customers to understand what they want, and helps developers understand how to build it better once they have done it the first time. The prototype is usually not used later — it is thrown away and new software is built.

blocks.caption: An early prototype helps the team understand requirements better.

blocks.text: Advantages: useful when the exact form of the solution and technical issues are unclear; useful to get feedback from customers.
Disadvantages: increased development cost (prototypes usually aren't reused); since we are not building the actual system, risks and bugs that appear later in the development cycle are not captured.
The prototype model belongs to the Plan and Document perspective.
REMEMBER  A prototype is a small working sample for early feedback, not the full product.

sections.title: Spiral Model: refine through repeated rounds

blocks.text: The spiral model combines the waterfall model and the prototyping model. We incrementally build the software, get feedback and refine.

blocks.caption: Each loop: determine objectives → evaluate risks → develop and test (show to client) → plan next phase.

rows: Determine objectives, alternatives and constraints for this iteration
Evaluate alternatives, identify and resolve risks
Develop and test, and release the product to the client

blocks.text: At each iteration the prototype is refined compared to the previous version.

Unlike the waterfall model, where everything is documented at the beginning, requirement documents are developed across iterations as and when they are needed, and the software eventually evolves into the final product. Customers are involved at the end of every iteration, which reduces misunderstandings between the client and the developers. Drawback: iterations still take a long time — around 6 to 24 months each.
REMEMBER  Spiral = planned iterations + explicit risk evaluation + customer feedback.
Models in the Plan and Document perspective: Waterfall, Prototype, Spiral

blocks.caption: Waterfall, Prototype and Spiral are Plan and Document models; XP, Scrum and Kanban are Agile approaches.

sections.title: Agile: working software, feedback and change

blocks.text: Plan and document processes brought discipline to software development, but they were not very effective at on-time delivery within budget. Studies of software projects from 1995 to 2013 show that 80–90% of all software projects were late, over budget or simply abandoned, and only about 10–15% were on time and on budget.

rows: 53% late/over budget/missing function; 31% terminated or abandoned
20% late/over budget; 70% major delays or terminated
52% late/over budget/missing function; 38% terminated or abandoned

blocks.text: To address these problems, in February 2001 a group of software developers met to develop a lighter-weight software development lifecycle, which came to be known as the Agile Manifesto.
4 key principles

blocks.caption: 4 key principles: people, working software, collaboration and change.

rows: Interactions within the team and with clients
Collaborate with the customer to understand their exact needs

blocks.text: Although the items on the right are valuable, the items on the left are more valuable in Agile.
Iterative / incremental development

Agile builds software through multiple iterations, so it is known as an iterative or incremental software development model: teams deliver the product in small increments. Instead of waiting till the end, teams develop prototypes of key features and quickly release them for feedback.

blocks.caption: Incremental development: planning → requirements → analysis & design → implementation → testing → evaluation, repeated; then deployment.

blocks.text: EXAMPLE  In the first iteration the team builds features for key requirements, shows them to the client and gets feedback. Even if the client wants changes, the team can quickly refine it in the next iteration.

blocks.caption: Small increments allow the customer to see progress and respond early.

blocks.text: REMEMBER  Agile follows the 4 key principles; short releases and constant feedback are ways to apply them.
The course introduces three Agile approaches.

blocks.caption: XP focuses on coding practices; Scrum organizes teamwork in short sprints.

rows: One of the earliest agile approaches; key practices include Behavior Driven Design, test driven development and pair programming
The product is built in a series of iterations called sprints, roughly 1–2 weeks long, breaking a big complex project into smaller bite-sized pieces
The work is divided into small work items represented on a Kanban board, so team members can see the state of every piece of work at any given time

blocks.text: Agile practices

rows: A short statement of a user’s need
Iterations in which the team builds the product
Short team meetings to coordinate work
Write a test for desired behavior before writing code to make it pass

blocks.caption: XP practices: pair programming, test driven development, behavior driven design.

blocks.text: In this course, practices from XP and Scrum — behavior driven design, test driven development, sprints — are used for the group projects.
Kanban: see work moving across a board
A Kanban board shows the state of every work item at any given time.

blocks.caption: Example Kanban workflow: To Do → In Progress → Testing → Done.

blocks.text: Agile philosophy: Rather than just following approaches and practices, Agile is about adhering to the broad philosophy — the 4 key principles — and using them to figure out the right things to do in your particular context.

sections.title: How do we choose a development approach?

blocks.text: Mostly YES answers suggest Plan and Document; mostly NO answers suggest Agile.

blocks.caption: Waterfall vs Agile at a glance.
Mostly YES → Plan and Document; mostly NO → Agile.

blocks.text: A no answer suggests Agile; a yes suggests Plan and Document

rows: Is the system to be built large?
Is the system to be built complex (e.g., real time)?
Will it have a long product lifetime?
Are you using poor software tools?
Is the project team geographically distributed?
Is team part of a documentation-oriented culture?
Does the team have poor programming skills?
Is the system to be built subject to regulation?

blocks.text: I. Sommerville, Software Engineering, Ninth Edition, Addison-Wesley, 2010.
If requirements/specifications must be fixed upfront → Plan and Document. If clients are unavailable most of the time → Plan and Document.
Large or very complex systems such as an air missile system or a nuclear power plant have no margin for error, so extensive planning and documentation are necessary.
If the team is geographically distributed or already familiar with a documentation model → Plan and Document.
Systems subject to regulation, e.g. banking software that needs approvals from banks and the government, need upfront planning and documentation.

The approach depends on the clients, the characteristics of the system and the team. Once you work in a software company, different teams and organisations will use different processes based on these factors.
REMEMBER  Pick an approach based on the client, the system and the team - not just a fashionable method.

blocks.text: Eight quick concept checks
1.  A payment function works alone but fails when called by the shopping cart. Which testing level is needed?  Answer: Integration testing.
2.  An employee portal is built for a company’s HR department. Is the client external?  Answer: No, internal.
3.  A developer changes a function’s input and another module breaks. Which agreement was changed?  Answer: Its interface.
4.  A client cannot describe the screens they want. What can help them respond early?  Answer: A working prototype.
5.  An iteration begins by listing options and evaluating possible failures. Which model makes risk evaluation explicit?  Answer: Spiral.
6. Which models belong to the Plan and Document perspective? → Waterfall, Prototype, Spiral.
7. Who conducts alpha testing, and where? → Internal employees, in a lab/staging environment.
8. Mostly 'yes' answers to Sommerville's 10 questions suggest which approach? → Plan and Document.
